stature.source: typical: the drafter's estimate for Sierra trees, which are much shorter than northern ones (the Gymnosperm Database gives 30-70 m range-wide); tall: the largest tree by size, near Lake Tahoe, 39 m tall and 263 cm dbh; record height: the Idaho champion, 69.8 m (1992 measurement) (Gymnosperm Database); read 2026-11-04

targets.from: judgement values from the drafter's reading of the sources and knowledge of the species (2026-11-04), no photographs measured; to be replaced by photo measurements: a narrow, open crown of well-spaced, slightly upswept limbs; old trees broad-topped and lopsided on granite; blue-green with a silvery cast

pole.note: a young tree: a narrow, open cone on a thin, smooth grey trunk

old-growth.note: an old subalpine tree: a massive checkered trunk and a broad, flattened, open crown of long limbs

description: A five-needled pine of the high country, 15-35 m here, with slender blue-green needles that catch the light silvery, long curved cones like small sugar pine cones, and a trunk whose bark breaks into small squarish dark plates like a chessboard. It grows scattered on granite slopes and ridges of the upper red fir and lodgepole forests, about 2100-3200 m, often as lone wide-crowned old trees on rock.

season_notes.winter: Evergreen; the open crowns let the snow through to the rock below.
season_notes.spring: Pollen in June-July as the snow melts.
season_notes.summer: The slim cones hang from the upper branches, green then brown and resin-streaked.
season_notes.fall: Cones open and drop seed in September, then fall whole; they are often sticky with white resin.

range.where: granite slopes of the upper montane and subalpine: May Lake, Tenaya Lake, Tioga Road, Glacier Point Road's upper end

notes: Distinguished from the ponderosa template by its short (4-10 cm) five-needle bundles, bluer colour, narrow open crown, and above all the checkered bark of old trees, which the Gymnosperm Database calls unlike any other North American tree; the bark pattern 'checkered' is the nearest the generator has. Young trees have thin smooth grey bark (set on the pole class). Cones 10-25 cm, hanging, not drawn. Blister rust kills many in the Sierra. Seeds feed chickarees, chipmunks and nutcrackers, none in the animal library; Steller's jay stands in. Sierra elevations: the Gymnosperm Database gives about 1900-3000 m in the southern part of the range; the central Sierra belt here is the drafter's knowledge.
